title: Influence of Zoroastrianism on Judaism (typescript by Shaul Shaked, Exhibit I in Tanenbaum Collection folder 'Zoroastrianism, 1984')
venue: American Jewish Archives, MS-603 Rabbi Marc H. Tanenbaum Collection, Box 53 Folder 10
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: scholars of Iranian generally tend to assume that Iran had a great deal of influence on Judaism and Christianity
summary: Shaked, an Iranist, names angelology/demonology, eschatology and dualism as the changes in post-exilic Judaism that point to Persia and notes Persian loanwords in Hebrew and Aramaic books. He also says Iranian and Jewish dualism are 'not really the same system'.
limits: Typescript of a script prepared for a lay or interfaith audience (the cover note says Shaked was 'contacted'; authorship and date are not otherwise stated beyond the 1984 folder). OCR text has errors. He states a possible source, not a documented route; he concedes the Jewish system 'is basically monotheist'.

strand.what: angelology/demonology, eschatology and dualism (plus Persian loanwords)

title: Zoroastrianism and Biblical Religion
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: not a single Persian loanword is known throughout the entirety of the Hebrew Torah
summary: A sceptical survey that goes item by item (dualism, Satan, creation, purity, angels, resurrection) and argues that sweeping claims of Zoroastrian influence on biblical theology are not supported, and that Zoroastrian sources are too late.
limits: A cursory survey by his own account ('a cursory survey'); written against the 'minimalist' Persian-era dating of the Bible, which shapes its framing. Cites Boyce, Eichrodt and Shaked at second hand. Does not engage later Second Temple texts such as Qumran dualism at length.

strand.what: dualism, Satan, angelology, resurrection, creation theology

title: Zoroastrianism and Biblical Religion (Isbell quoting Shaul Shaked on chronology)
authors: Shaked, S. (quoted by Isbell, C. D.)
venue: Jewish Bible Quarterly 34(3) (second-hand: Shaked is quoted, not read in the original)
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: All arguments about possible contacts between Israel and Iran come to the stumbling block of the problem of chronology.
summary: Shaked, a proponent in his own lecture, is quoted by Isbell as stating the central chronological limit: detailed Zoroastrian theology survives only in Sasanian-era or later books.
limits: SECOND-HAND: the original Shaked source is not named in the text I opened and I did not read it. Isbell uses it for a sceptical purpose; Shaked's own overall position is more favourable to influence (see his typescript).

title: Zoroastrianism and Biblical Religion (Isbell reporting Mary Boyce on angelology)

quote: reflects to a large extent Zoroastrian belief in the yazatas
summary: Isbell reports Boyce as arguing that Jewish angelology (from the 'host of the heavens') reflects Zoroastrian yazatas, and then rebuts it because the yazatas were deities, not servants of Ahura Mazda.

title: Was Resurrection a Zoroastrian Idea? (Bremmer quoted by Bart Ehrman)
ask_addressed: Open the scholarship on whether Persian (Zoroastrian) ideas shaped Judaism: Barr, 'The Question of Religious Influence: The Case of Zoroastrianism, Judaism, and Christianity' (JAAR 1985), Mary Boyce, Grabbe on the Persian period, Bremmer 2002, Mark S. Smith 2001, and any open-access review article.
quote: There … is little reason to derive Jewish ideas about resurrection from Persian sources. Their origin(s) may well lie in intra-Jewish developments
summary: Ehrman quotes Bremmer's conclusion (The Rise and Fall of the Afterlife, Routledge 2002, p. 59) and his point that the oldest Avesta manuscript dates from 1288 CE and all surviving copies derive from a 9th-10th century CE copy.
limits: SECOND-HAND: Bremmer's book is on archive.org but only as a lending-library copy, whose text I could not open. A blog post, dated by its page, with reader comments on the same page; the quote is in Ehrman's own text. Confined to resurrection.

title: Was Resurrection a Zoroastrian Idea? (Ehrman's chronology argument)
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: Do we see any evidence of a belief in resurrection in Jewish texts from that period? Well, actually, no we don’t.
summary: Ehrman argues from dating: Persian rule ended in the 4th century BCE but resurrection appears in Jewish texts only from the Maccabean period, so contact and the idea do not line up.
limits: A blog answer, not peer-reviewed; the page mixes Ehrman's text with reader comments and I could not fully separate them, so authorship of this passage is attributed on the page's apparent structure. A chronology argument, not a refutation: it does not rule out later transmission.

title: The Origins of Biblical Monotheism: Israel's Polytheistic Background and the Ugaritic Texts (author's summary)
venue: The Bible and Interpretation (University of Arizona), Dec. 2001
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: the conditions of human empires provided the model for divine empire
summary: Smith's own short summary of his book places the emergence of Israelite monotheism in the 7th-6th centuries BCE and explains it by social change and Assyrian and Babylonian empire, with Cyrus mentioned only as 'the Lord's anointed'.
limits: FIRST-HAND but only Smith's popular summary of the book, not the book's chapter on Isaiah 40-55 (OUP page is paywalled). The summary does not discuss Persian religion; his view on Zoroastrianism comes only second-hand via Antia.

strand.what: model of a single god ruling all nations

title: Views of Scholars Refuting Zoroastrian Influence (excerpting M. S. Smith, 2001)
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: this is not to say that Persian religious tradition did not reinforce monotheistic rhetoric in this period
summary: Antia quotes Smith as doubting that Zoroastrian dualism was the model for biblical monotheism, while conceding Persian religion may have reinforced monotheistic rhetoric; Smith's main source for monotheism is the older Israelite and Ugaritic background.
limits: SECOND-HAND for Smith (book not opened). Antia is a Zoroastrian priest and an advocate; the essay selects and comments, and its quotations were not checked against Smith. Kept second-hand.

title: Views of Scholars Refuting Zoroastrian Influence (excerpting R. C. Zaehner)
authors: Antia, K. (quoting Zaehner, R. C., The Dawn and Twilight of Zoroastrianism)
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: Zoroaster’s doctrine of rewards and punishments, of an eternity of bliss and an eternity of woe
summary: Zaehner, as quoted, finds direct influence 'surely' for the individual afterlife and rewards and punishments.
limits: SECOND-HAND (Zaehner's book not opened). The same excerpt has Zaehner calling the case for eschatology 'not at all convincing' for lack of evidence from the last four centuries BCE; the quoted sentence stands for the proponent's strongest line. Antia is an advocate.

title: Views of Scholars Refuting Zoroastrian Influence (Zaehner on the limits of the evidence)

quote: We cannot say with any certainty whether the Jews borrowed from the Zoroastrians or the Zoroastrians from the Jews
summary: Zaehner, as quoted, calls a Judaeo-Christian dependence on Zoroastrian eschatology 'not at all convincing' because no eschatological evidence survives for the last four centuries BCE.
limits: SECOND-HAND (Zaehner's book not opened). Antia then disagrees in his own comment.

quote: it can hardly be denied that the apocalyptic teaching, for example, concerning such matters as the two ages

title: Hesiodic reminiscences in Zoroastrian-Hellenistic apocalypses (footnote on Gignoux)
ask_addressed: Quote the strongest proponent and the strongest sceptic first-hand, with their stated reasons and limits.
quote: Persian apocalyptic is either too late to be taken as an effective influence on its Jewish counterpart
summary: A proponent of Persian influence (his page is open only for abstract, footnotes and references) reports the late-dating sceptic position (Gignoux) and Mesopotamian-origin alternatives (Kvanvig, Burkert).
limits: The quoted footnote is Dobroruka's report; Gignoux's own papers were not opened (SECOND-HAND). Full article is behind a paywall; I opened abstract, footnotes and references only. Dobroruka is himself author of a pro-influence book.
